source_read: PMC HTML (PMC3427723, author manuscript; Drug Alcohol Depend 2012;125:230-238): structured abstract, Introduction, Methods 2.1-2.5, Results 3.1-3.4 with Tables 1-3 and Figure 1-2 legends, Discussion, Acknowledgments/role of funding, footnotes (contributors, conflict of interest). The supplementary .docx (caudate ROI analysis, Supplemental Table 1) was not opened (download only); its results are taken from the main-text summary.

claims.overstatement: 'Only 4 of 10 regional differences remained when users were compared with smoking controls' misdescribes Table 2. Users (all smokers) differed from non-smoking controls in 10 clusters and from smoking controls in 4 clusters, but the 4 are mostly at different locations: left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal and left precentral gyri. Only the left precentral cluster has a same-named counterpart among the 10 (peaks about 14 mm apart); the left superior temporal peak lies about 15 mm from the left insula cluster; the right inferior temporal and right supramarginal clusters have no counterpart. The authors' own summary is that, of the cingulate, superior temporal, insula and DLPFC differences reported in earlier studies, only superior temporal remained significant against smoking controls (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Suggested wording: 'users had smaller grey matter than non-smoking controls in 10 clusters but than smoking controls in only 4, mostly different, temporal, parietal and precentral clusters'.
claims.note: Supported from this source: smaller grey matter in frontal (orbitofrontal, superior frontal, frontal pole, precentral), cingulate, insular, temporal and parietal regions and caudate in users vs non-smoking controls; non-using smokers also had smaller right orbitofrontal grey matter than non-smokers (and smaller caudate in a supplementary ROI analysis); no relation of methamphetamine or cigarette exposure measures to grey matter; the authors state they did not replicate the hippocampal finding of Thompson et al. (2004). Further qualifications: education was lower in users (12.8 vs 14.6/14.1 years) and was not in the model; with education added, results held only at p<0.005 uncorrected (Discussion, limitations). All users smoked, so methamphetamine effects in non-smokers cannot be estimated. Longitudinal grey-matter increases over about 3.5 weeks of abstinence (12 vs 12) are at p<0.001 uncorrected.

anchors.locator: Results 3.2, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Control Nonsmoker > MA-Dependent Smoker)
anchors.extracted: 18 non-smoking controls vs 39 methamphetamine-dependent smokers (4-7 days abstinent). VBM, ANCOVA with age, sex and cannabis frequency; voxel p<0.001, cluster FWE p<0.05. Ten clusters smaller in users: right frontal pole/orbitofrontal, left orbitofrontal, left superior frontal, left insula, left and right precentral, right middle temporal, right precuneus, left caudate, right cingulate.

anchors.locator: Results 3.2; Table 2 (Control Nonsmoker > Control Tobacco Smoker); Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: 25 smoking controls vs 18 non-smoking controls: smokers had smaller right orbitofrontal grey matter (one cluster, 1043 voxels, T 5.59, FWE p<0.001); no other difference. Users and smoking controls did not differ in right orbitofrontal volume. Supplementary caudate tracing: smoking controls and users both smaller than non-smokers, no difference between them (summary in main text).

anchors.locator: Results 3.2; Table 2 (Control Tobacco Smoker > MA-Dependent Smoker); Discussion, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Against smoking controls, users had smaller grey matter in 4 clusters: left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal and left precentral gyri; no region where smoking controls were smaller. Authors: of the cingulate, superior temporal, insula and DLPFC differences consistent with earlier studies, only superior temporal remained significant against smoking controls.

anchors.locator: Results 3.2, last sentence of 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Measures of cigarette smoking and methamphetamine use (days, grams/week, years, age at first use; pack-years, Fagerstrom) not significantly related to grey matter. Authors: could reflect abnormalities that predate drug use, or a threshold/multifactorial relation.
Authors state they did not replicate their laboratory's earlier finding of smaller hippocampal volume in users (Thompson et al., 2004), possibly because of different methods.

Education lower in users (12.8 vs 14.6 and 14.1 years, F(2,79)=8.52, p<0.001); mother's education not different. Education was not a covariate; with education in the model the results were reproduced only at p<0.005 uncorrected.

12 users vs 12 controls rescanned after 23.5 (SD 1.6) and 31.6 (SD 13.1) days. Group-by-time interactions (p<0.001 uncorrected, >=100 voxels) in bilateral superior temporal, right angular, right insula, left precuneus, left inferior frontal, left occipital pole (increases in users) and left cerebellum (decrease); no change in controls at that threshold.

key_findings.correction: Results 3.2, last sentence of 1st paragraph is right; the Discussion statement (no significant relationship between drug exposure and grey matter; may reflect premorbid abnormalities) is in the 5th paragraph, not the 3rd.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently; implied p values 0.0135 and 0.0031 recomputed.
The sentence on 60% overlap with Tabibnia et al. (2011) follows the description of the longitudinal groups but is ambiguous about which groups it refers to.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree it is the strongest structural study in the batch, but 'moderate' is a ROBINS-I label; ROBINS-E uses low / some concerns / high / very high. For the question the encyclopedia asks (does methamphetamine cause the grey-matter differences), confounding is still high under ROBINS-E: education (about 1.5-1.8 years lower) is not in the main model and holds only at p<0.005 uncorrected when added, no pre-use data, and all users smoke. I would rate confounding 'high' and overall 'high', with the card's reasoning that tobacco, the main named confounder, is addressed by design.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor overall; the recovery inference in the abstract is the weakest link (uncorrected longitudinal analysis, 12 per group).

missed: Discussion, 4th paragraph says users had smaller cingulate, superior temporal, insula and DLPFC grey matter than non-smoking controls, but the Control Nonsmoker > user list (Results 3.2; Table 2) contains neither superior temporal gyrus nor DLPFC; superior temporal appears only in the three-group ANCOVA and the smoking-control comparison.

Discussion, final (strengths) paragraph calls the caudate and parietal deficits 'uniquely associated with early abstinence from MA', although the paper's own supplementary ROI analysis and abstract show the caudate deficit in non-using smokers as well.

The 4 clusters distinguishing users from smoking controls (left superior temporal, right inferior temporal, right supramarginal, left precentral) are mostly not the same regions as the 10 distinguishing users from non-smokers: only left precentral has a same-named counterpart (peaks 13.6 mm apart), the left superior temporal peak is 14.5 mm from the left insula peak, and the right inferior temporal and supramarginal clusters have no counterpart. This matters for cl_meth_grey_matter, which says '4 of 10 regional differences remained'.

Conflict-of-interest footnote and supplement aside, London et al. (2015) reproduce this paper's longitudinal map with a legend giving p<0.005 uncorrected and >200 voxels, whereas this paper's Methods 2.5 give p<0.001 uncorrected and >=100 voxels (minor cross-source inconsistency).
